profile_md:
## Seven Seas Water Group - Water-as-a-Service operator (not a chemical supplier)

**Overview.** Seven Seas Water Group (Tampa, FL and Houston, TX) designs, finances, builds, owns and operates decentralized water and wastewater treatment plants under long-term, take-or-pay, inflation-linked contracts it brands "Water-as-a-Service(R)". It sells treated water by the gallon (seawater and brackish reverse osmosis desalination, surface-water treatment) and wastewater treatment capacity (packaged/modular plants leased or sold through its AUC Group subsidiary). It runs more than 220 plants across the US, the Caribbean and Latin America. The company says it produces about 20 billion gallons of treated water a year and treats about 150 million gallons of wastewater a day. **For a water treatment chemicals map it is a customer, not a competitor.** It buys antiscalants, coagulants, chlorine/hypochlorite, pH chemicals and membrane cleaners for its plants, and it does not make or resell chemicals as a business line. It belongs in the universe as a *Water utility / O&M operator* and a demand-side account.

**History & ownership.** Founded in 1997 in the US Virgin Islands. It became part of AquaVenture Holdings, which listed on the NYSE as WAAS in October 2016 with two segments, Seven Seas Water (SSW) and Quench. On 1 Nov 2018 AquaVenture bought AUC Group, a Houston decentralized-wastewater company founded in 1970, from NewSpring Capital and Argosy for about $130M. On 30 Mar 2020 Culligan (then Advent/BC Partners-backed) took AquaVenture private for about $1.1B EV, kept Quench, and sold Seven Seas Water the same day to Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners (MSIP). The price was not disclosed. Trade press reports it at about $500M. Under MSIP the company bought Aguas de Panama from Sembcorp (Nov 2020: a 20 MGD Lake Gatun plant on a 30-year IDAAN concession serving about 420k people). It refinanced with a $205M Deutsche Bank/Investec syndicated loan in 2021, won the City of Alice (TX) BWRO and South Texas Water Authority (Robstown, TX) contracts, a 20-year Aqualectra BOOT in Curaçao (2024), and new Antigua (APUA) plants and an Aruba (WEB) project. Through AUC it bought the WAWCON clarifier assets in Oct 2024. On 22 May 2025 EQT Infrastructure VI agreed to buy the company from MSIP. Bloomberg reported a value of "more than $1 billion, including debt". RBC advised the seller and A&O Shearman advised EQT.

**Products & chemistries.** It has no chemical product lines. Its service lines are (1) bulk potable/industrial water from SWRO/BWRO and conventional plants; (2) wastewater treatment plant rental and leasing plus plant/equipment sales (AUC); and (3) financing of customer-owned plants. Chemicals are an operating cost within opex, bought from third parties such as membrane-chemical, coagulant and hypochlorite suppliers.

**End markets & customers.** The main customers are government utilities and water authorities: USVI WAPA historically, BVI, Anguilla, Trinidad, Curaçao Aqualectra, Antigua APUA, Aruba WEB, Panama IDAAN, and Texas municipalities and water authorities. Other customers are hospitality/resort developers (Turks & Caicos, Bahamas, Sint Maarten), industrial and mining users (Aguas de Bayovar, which supplies Vale's phosphate mine in Peru), and US property developers, MUDs, RV parks, schools and industrial sites served by AUC's packaged wastewater plants. The end-market split in this file is an analyst estimate.

**Footprint.** Corporate offices are at 14400 Carlson Circle, Tampa, FL 33626 and in Houston, TX (AUC). US plants are concentrated in Texas (the AUC decentralized wastewater fleet, Alice, Robstown/STWA) and the US Virgin Islands. International plants are in Anguilla, Antigua & Barbuda, Aruba, Bahamas, BVI, Curaçao, Panama, Peru, Sint Maarten, Trinidad and Turks & Caicos.

**Financials.** The last disclosed figures are for FY2019 (AquaVenture 10-K/earnings): SSW revenue of $88.3M (bulk water $60.5M, rental $14.8M, product sales $9.4M, financing $3.7M) and Adjusted EBITDA of $46.7M (53% margin). The plant count grew from about 100 (2021) to more than 220 (2025), and annual water output from 8.5bn gallons (mid-2019) to about 20bn gallons. That growth came mainly from Panama (20 MGD, about 7bn gal/yr), new Antigua plants and Texas. **Estimate** for 2025: revenue about $145M (range $120-175M) and EBITDA about $70M (about 48%). The EBITDA estimate cross-checks against the >$1B EV at a 14-16x infrastructure multiple. US revenue is estimated at about 40%, or about $58M (AUC plus Texas bulk water plus USVI). Revenue from water treatment chemicals is zero.

**M&A strategy.** It buys contracted, cash-yielding water assets and concessions: AUC in 2018 and APSA Panama in 2020. It also does tuck-ins for capability (WAWCON clarifiers, 2024) and advertises that it will buy existing water and wastewater plants. EQT is expected to push US decentralized wastewater and municipal P3 growth.

**Competitive position.** Its competitors are other BOO/P3 water providers and O&M firms rather than chemical companies: Veolia, Jacobs/Inframark, Aqua/Essential's decentralized business, Consolidated Water (Caribbean desal), IDE and Acciona in Caribbean desal, and local packaged-plant vendors. Its moat is a 20+ year record of long-term take-or-pay contracts and financing capability.

**Risks.** Contracts are concentrated with small island governments, where payment and sovereign credit risk apply (arrears have been an issue in past USVI and Caribbean utility contracts). There is hurricane exposure, re-tender risk at contract expiry, leverage under infrastructure ownership, and execution risk on Texas desal P3s.

**Uncertainties.** No revenue or EBITDA has been disclosed since 2019. The 2025 figures here are estimates, the EQT EV is press-reported, the employee count is unverified, and the number of US plants is not disclosed.
